title: Studying in Germany for free: the 2027 guide for Uzbek and Kazakh students
summary: How to check direct entry or Studienkolleg, whether APS applies, how to prove funds with a blocked account, and what a realistic budget looks like.

sources.title: Federal Foreign Office: visa rules, blocked account (Sperrkonto)

review_note: Verified on fetched official pages: the Federal Foreign Office page (blocked account amount varies by purpose and is set by the competent mission; no figure published there, so no amount is stated in the article) and the uni-assist Uzbekistan page (admission details come from each university). Not verified, so phrased without numbers or rules: the APS country list, Studienkolleg routes for 11-year certificates, the semester contribution, and the blocked account amount. The uni-assist and DAAD citations are homepage-level; their deep pages returned 403/404 or a bot-check at check time.
body:
## In short

- Many German public universities charge no tuition for bachelor's study, but tuition rules differ by state and by university, so check the programme page.
- You still pay a semester contribution and must budget for living costs, which is the biggest expense.
- Before you apply, confirm three things: whether your school certificate gives direct entry or sends you to a Studienkolleg, whether you need an APS certificate, and how you will prove your funds.
- Requirements change, so confirm amounts and rules with the German mission in Tashkent or Astana and the university before you pay anything.

## Why "free" needs a closer look

"Free" usually means no tuition fee at a public university. It does not mean no cost. You will pay a semester contribution, which covers student services and often a transport ticket, and you will pay rent, food, health insurance and study materials. For a student from Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan, the money you must show at the visa stage is the figure that sets your real budget.

Some German states charge tuition to non-EU students, and some universities charge fees for specific programmes, such as private universities or certain master's courses. Check the tuition section on each university's international page, not only a general country guide.

## Step 1: Check whether you enter directly or through a Studienkolleg

A German university decides whether your school leaving certificate qualifies you for a bachelor's programme directly. If it does not, you normally attend a Studienkolleg, a one-year preparatory course that ends with a qualifying exam (the Feststellungsprüfung). Many students from Central Asia ask this question first, and the answer depends on your certificate, your subject and your university.

The uni-assist service, which many universities use to check foreign applications, publishes country information and says that official admission information comes from each university's own website. Read that page, then email the admissions office with a copy of your certificate and ask in writing which route applies to your subject.

## Step 2: Ask about APS

The APS certificate is an authentication document issued by the German-run APS office in each applicant country. Some applicant groups must obtain it before a visa interview. Official guidance does not settle the list for every country in one place, so do not assume your nationality is exempt or required. Ask the German mission and your target university directly, and get the answer in writing. If APS applies, apply early, because the process takes time.

## Step 3: Language

Most bachelor's programmes in Germany are taught in German. Universities commonly ask for a German language certificate at a level such as B2 or C1, depending on the programme. Some programmes are taught in English. Those usually require an English test, which you can read about in the separate article on English tests. Do not choose an English-taught programme only because you think the German language requirement is too hard. Check the course language, the entry test and the living costs in the same city.

## Step 4: Proving your money

Non-EU students usually show proof of sufficient funds at the visa stage. The most common route is a blocked account, known in German as a Sperrkonto. The German Federal Foreign Office says the amount varies depending on the purpose of your stay and is based on the maximum rates for support received by German students. It also says the exact figure is set out by the competent mission abroad, and that the Consular Services Portal is the place to confirm it.

Practical steps:

- Ask the German mission for the current year's amount before you open any account.
- Compare the amount and the monthly withdrawal rules across the providers the mission recognises.
- Keep bank statements and the confirmation letter together.
- Ask whether a scholarship award letter can replace the blocked account. Scholarship rules are specific, so get the answer from the mission or the scholarship provider, not from a blog.

Do not transfer money to a relative to show on your statement. Visa officers look at the origin and history of funds, and a sudden deposit raises questions.

## Step 5: Timing

German intakes usually start in the winter semester (October) or the summer semester (April). Application deadlines differ by university, and some use uni-assist. Your visa appointment can take weeks to schedule, and the blocked account and APS steps can take longer than you expect. Work backwards from the start date. A realistic plan begins at least six months before your intended start.

## What a realistic budget looks like

Build your budget from categories rather than from a single headline figure:

- Semester contribution, as stated by your university.
- Rent for a room in a shared flat, using the local housing listings for your city.
- Food, transport and phone.
- Health insurance, which German student visa rules require you to have.
- Study materials and any Studienkolleg fees.
- A buffer for the first month, before any part-time work starts.

Part-time work is limited for students from outside the EU, and rules on hours and eligibility apply. Check the official conditions for your visa type before you plan to rely on it.

## Common mistakes

- Applying to a programme without checking whether it is taught in German or English.
- Assuming a Studienkolleg is optional when the university has said it is required.
- Opening a blocked account without first checking the current amount.
- Sending documents to a university without certified copies or translations when it asks for them.
- Missing an APS or language certificate deadline because it was not on the checklist.

## Questions to ask the admissions office

A short email with precise questions gets better answers than a long one. Ask the admissions office:

- Does my school leaving certificate give direct access to this bachelor's programme, or is a Studienkolleg required?
- Is APS needed for my nationality, and at which step do you check it?
- Which German language certificate do you accept, and what level does the programme require at the start?
- Do you need certified copies, translations or an apostille for my school records?
- What is the semester contribution for this year, and does it include a transport ticket?
- Is there a deadline for the application through uni-assist, and a separate deadline for the university?

Keep the replies in writing. If the answer differs between two staff members, ask the one responsible for your programme to confirm.

## Living in a German city

Housing is the first hurdle. Student residences are often allocated by a waiting list, so apply to them early, then look at private shared flats as a backup. Local listings and student services offices publish typical rents for each city. Use those figures rather than a national average.

Health insurance is compulsory for students in Germany. Students from outside the EU usually need a policy that the German health and visa rules accept, and the university's international office can explain which providers are common. Keep the insurance certificate with your visa documents.

Register your address within the time set by the city. Many students find that the registration office, the bank and the health insurer all ask for the same document, so keep several certified copies of your residence registration.

## Keeping your student status

German universities set the number of semesters you need to complete and the exams you must pass each year. Missing exams can lead to the loss of your place, which can affect your residence permit. Check the rules at the start of each semester and keep your enrolment certificate up to date. Your residence permit is tied to your studies, so tell the foreigners' office if you change programme or university.

## Checklist

- [ ] Confirm direct entry or Studienkolleg for your certificate in writing.
- [ ] Ask the German mission whether APS applies to your nationality.
- [ ] Confirm the current blocked account amount on the Consular Services Portal or the mission site.
- [ ] Check the semester contribution and any tuition rules on each university's page.
- [ ] Choose the course language and the matching language certificate.
- [ ] Book the visa appointment as early as the mission allows.
- [ ] Build a budget by category and keep a one-month buffer.
- [ ] Keep certified copies and translations of every school record.
